analysis.one_liner: Guaranteed health coverage for every American with capped premiums and out-of-pocket limits, financed by employer and family payments.
analysis.headline: The bill that embodied the Clinton administration's universal health care plan was introduced by Senator Kennedy with no cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or floor vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have entitled everyone legally in the United States to a comprehensive health benefit package — hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, mental health care, dental and vision care, and preventive services — with annual out-of-pocket costs capped at $1,500 per person and $3,000 per family. No plan could turn anyone down or charge more for a preexisting condition, and a new National Health Board would cap how fast premiums could grow. Families and employers would pay premiums on a sliding scale, with low-income families getting discounts. It was the Senate version of President Clinton's Health Security Act.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 37 million uninsured Americans at the time, plus everyone at risk of losing coverage when changing jobs or getting sick. People with preexisting conditions could no longer be denied or priced out of coverage, low-income families would get reduced premiums and cost sharing, and every enrollee would get a guaranteed rich benefit package no matter where they worked or lived.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every citizen, legal permanent resident, and long-term nonimmigrant to a comprehensive benefit package through a health plan, and bars plans from refusing enrollment for health status, preexisting conditions, or any personal characteristic.
Caps annual out-of-pocket expenses at $1,500 for an individual and $3,000 for a family, and reduces cost sharing and premiums for low-income families.
Requires regional alliances to offer a choice of health plans including at least one fee-for-service option, and lets states opt to run a single-payer system with federal approval.

Limits premium growth through regional alliance inflation factors and per-capita premium targets set by the National Health Board, and terminates corporate alliances whose cost growth repeatedly exceeds national targets.
Adds new long-term care benefits for people with disabilities and new public health, mental health, and community health center funding.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who must make premium payments for their employees scaled to payroll size and average wages; higher-income families, who pay a larger share of premiums on the income-related schedule; and the federal budget, which funds new long-term care, public health, and workforce programs and backstops alliance financing.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate requires businesses to make monthly premium payments for qualifying employees, with amounts varying by employer size and average wages — a new cost that small business groups and many employers opposed.

A seven-member National Health Board appointed by the President would set premium targets, define benefits, and oversee cost containment — critics argued this concentrated sweeping pricing power in an executive-branch body.
Every eligible individual must enroll in a health plan and pay required premiums, making coverage compulsory rather than voluntary.

The bill excludes some services people expect — hearing aids, adult eyeglasses, in vitro fertilization, most orthodontia — and imposes annual limits on inpatient mental health and substance abuse treatment before 2001.
The measure ran to hundreds of pages creating alliances, boards, councils, and commissions, and opponents argued the administrative structure was too complex to implement as designed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was the most far-reaching universal coverage proposal ever to reach the Senate floor stage: guaranteed benefits, out-of-pocket caps, and an end to being turned down for being sick, financed by mandatory employer payments and income-scaled premiums. The genuine tradeoffs were real — new costs on employers of every size, a powerful federal board controlling premium growth, compulsory enrollment, and benefits not as rich as many existing plans in some categories. Whether those costs were worth ending medical bankruptcy and job-lock was the core dispute; the Senate never got far enough to weigh them in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 1993 and placed on the Senate calendar, it never got a committee hearing or a floor vote; after Senate leaders concluded in August 1994 that it lacked the votes, it sat until the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Health Security Act on November 22, 1993.
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 340, but no committee acted on it.
The only recorded action after introduction was sponsor introductory remarks on August 4, 1994; the bill never came to a vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers facing the premium mandate, pharmaceutical makers facing premium caps, and opponents of a government-run framework were better off because the bill never advanced; tens of millions of uninsured Americans remained without guaranteed coverage.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor in November 1993 and again in August 1994.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Proposed the Health Security Act as the centerpiece of his administration and campaigned publicly for congressional passage.

against.name: George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Concluded by August 1994 that the bill lacked majority support and never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: 44 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill unanimously and blocked it through unified resistance to the Clinton plan.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Health Insurance Association of America and its member insurers
against.what_they_did: Ran a nationally broadcast advertising campaign ('Harry and Louise') attacking the plan and lobbied heavily against it.

against.name: Small business groups
against.role: National Federation of Independent Business and allied employer associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the employer premium mandate as a new cost on small employers.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: Publicly predicted the plan would collapse and declined to move it through the Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party; Republicans opposed it unanimously while several moderate and conservative Democrats also broke with the plan, leaving it short of the votes needed on the Democratic side.

industries.note: The bill would have ended medical underwriting — plans had to accept every applicant at community-rated prices, could not cancel coverage, and had to bid against capped premium targets. Individual underwriting-based pricing, the industry's core business model, would effectively end.
Employers would owe monthly premium payments for every qualifying employee, scaled to size and wages, replacing voluntary decisions about whether and how generously to cover workers.
Even with premiums scaled by employer size and average wages, small employers would face new mandatory payments, which is why small business associations campaigned against the bill.

Universal coverage would end uncompensated care for the uninsured and the bill directs payments to hospitals serving low-income patients, but premium caps and per-capita payment targets would limit revenue growth.
Outpatient prescription drugs would become a covered benefit funded through capped premiums, and an Advisory Council on Breakthrough Drugs would examine the reasonableness of new-drug launch prices.

The bill imposes federal standards on long-term care policies — standardized terms, limits on preexisting-condition exclusions, sales-practice rules — while new public home and community-based benefits compete with the private product.
